extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of English literature; poets, critics, and literary historians
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and critical principles for assessing poetry (especially descriptive, pastoral, satiric, and lyric) and prose style across several English poets (Cowper, Bloomfield, Crabbe, Prior, Gay, Swift, Johnson, etc.). Emphasises word-choice, manner of description, moral imagination, plausibility, and stylistic adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of the properest word / idiomatic precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors 'looked about them for the properest word to convey any idea... only one of them the very word we want' — a perfection of pure conversational prose consists in having the whole range of familiar words at command and knowing which to choose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the single English word that answers exactly to the idea; attend to idiomatic peculiarities and the different shades of association attached to common words. The Arbuthnot/Queen Anne writers are praised for this careful selection; contrasted with Johnsonian habit of forced Latinate coinages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness and terseness
rubrics_metrics.description: Style that 'leaves out every superfluous word; is sparing of connecting particles, and introductory phrases' is a virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unnecessary verbiage and redundant connective tissue. A terse, concentrated style is preferable for clarity and native force (example: Arbuthnot).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of learned Latinized jargon ('sesquipedalia verba')
rubrics_metrics.description: Dr. Johnson's style is criticized for translating into the first Greek or Latin word he can think of, producing 'sesquipedalia verba' — learned words that impose sameness and a pompous sameness of effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not substitute foreignized learned diction for natural English expression; such jargon flattens variety and hinders perception of differences between subjects. Use learning sparingly and only where natural idiom fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of inflection and adaptation of style
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern learned prose 'wants variety of inflection and adaptation; it hinders us from seeing the differences of the things it undertakes to describe.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt register, rhythm, and syntactic inflection to the subject; avoid a one-note learned style. True excellence requires flexibility of tone and form appropriate to content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive poetry must be clothed by a 'moral imagination' (drapery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bloomfield 'gives the simple appearance of nature, but he gives it naked, shivering, and unclothed with the drapery of a moral imagination.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good description does more than record appearances: it clothes them with feeling, thought, or moral significance. The best descriptions (e.g. Milton's Lycidas, or The Winter's Tale) integrate scenery with imaginative and moral depth rather than offering bare literal detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-literal minuteness and inventorying of detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Crabbe 'gives the very costume of meanness... takes an inventory of the human heart exactly in the same manner as of the furniture of a sick room' — excessive minuteness produces inanimateness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Too much literal, documentary detail (cataloguing furniture, petty defects) drains life and warmth from poetry; description should preserve movement, feeling, and human vitality rather than museum-like petrifaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate description into a larger imaginative/moral vision
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The best descriptive poetry is not, after all, to be found in our descriptive poets.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptions work best when embedded in broader poetic purpose (myth, moral, imaginative narrative). Purely 'descriptive' poets may record appearances well but fail to produce the supreme descriptive effects achieved by poets whose description arises organically from larger themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pastoral requires suitable Arcadian conditions (manners, climate, age)
rubrics_metrics.description: We have few good pastorals because 'our manners are not Arcadian; our climate is not an eternal spring; our age is not the age of gold.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pastoral succeeds when the cultural and emotional material fits the idealized rural scheme; without an underlying compatibility of manners and imagination, pastoral risks affectation or failure. Walton's Complete Angler is singled out as successful because simplicity and piety support its pastoral effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of character and costume; plausibility and modesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Gay 'has effected this transformation without once violating probability, or "o'erstepping the modesty of nature." The preservation of the character and costume is complete.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When transmuting coarse or vulgar material into art, keep the characters true to type and the incident plausible; do not force manners or speech beyond their natural limits. Authenticity of costume and manner lends authority to satire and transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform vulgar materials into refined composition by wit and insight
rubrics_metrics.description: Gay 'extracts an essence of refinement from the dregs of human life' — the elegance of the composition is in exact proportion to the coarseness of the materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective art can elevate low subject-matter by judicious tone (mock-heroic, irony), refined diction where appropriate, and sympathetic insight into human feeling; the transformation must be achieved without violating nature or probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use wit to moderate the offensiveness of satire
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The very wit, however, takes off from the offensiveness of the satire.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire is more palatable and persuasive when delivered with wit and charm rather than merely with moral indignation; humour can humanise both satirist and subject and broaden audience sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity over affectation in sentimental or romantic writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior's 'sentimental and romantic productions are mere affectation, the result not of powerful impulse or real feeling, but of a consciousness of his deficiencies.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid manufactured sentiment or artifice meant to disguise lack of feeling or power. Genuine impulse and honest emotion trump laboured sentimentality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep fables and short moral pieces concise and pointed
rubrics_metrics.description: Gay's Fables are criticised as 'spun out too long; the descriptions and narrative are too diffuse and desultory; and the moral is sometimes without point.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fables need economy: brevity in narrative and clarity of moral point. Avoid diffuse description that dilutes the tale's point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple domestic detail can reveal piety and humanity
rubrics_metrics.description: In Walton's Complete Angler 'in the description of a fishing-tackle, you perceive the piety and humanity of the author's mind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully chosen humble details (household, craft, food) can communicate character, virtue, and humane feeling effectively. Illustrations or prints may add reality and interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evoke transferable, abstracted feeling in love-of-country subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinguishing element of our interest in the country is its 'abstractedness' — 'the interest we feel in external nature is common, and transferable from one object to all others of the same class.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evoke a generalized love of nature, build associative links so that feeling attached to one object extends to a class; employ remembrance, recurring motifs (sun, moon, flowers) and the idea of 'sameness' across time and place to produce an indissoluble attachment.
